Can I use a third-party solar panel with my power station? Yes, if the numbers match. The panels' open-circuit voltage (Voc) must sit inside the station's input range, below the maximum even on a cold morning, the current must stay under the input limit, and the plug must fit the solar port, directly or through an adapter cable rated for that current. The station's solar input limit tells you how many panel watts are worth buying. The solar charging calculator runs the voltage check for series wiring. A "solar generator" sounds like a distinct category of gear. It isn't. Every solar generator on the market is a portable power station bundled with one or more solar panels, sold under a single SKU at a single price. The marketing term is convenient — you search once, buy once, and everything theoretically works together out of the box. But because you're really buying two separate products wrapped in one listing, you can price-check the components individually and frequently find a better deal, a better panel, or both for the same money.
What a Solar Generator Bundle Actually Is Strip away the branding and every solar generator kit contains exactly two things: a battery-equipped power station with AC outlets and a foldable solar panel with the matching connector. Brands like Anker, Jackery, and EcoFlow package their own stations with their own panels, assign a new model number to the pair, and list it as a complete "solar generator."

Is a solar generator different from a power station? No. A solar generator is a marketing term for a power station bundled with a solar panel. The power station is the battery-and-inverter unit with AC outlets. The solar panel recharges it. You can buy them together as a "solar generator" kit or separately and pair them yourself.
